case_study_insert.main_stem: Valle Dorado Olive Oil (VDO) is a private limited company in the olive oil production and bottling sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2007 by Catalina Reyes, the business presses and bottles single-estate extra virgin olive oil for supermarket supply across three export markets and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VDO plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated bottling and filtration line with eco-friendly glass packaging, financed by a $650,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $288,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.20 a unit and a selling price of $14.60, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. VDO faces two problems: quality complaints about sediment in unfiltered bottles have reached 26 per month, and its warehouse has reported rising spillage waste.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2026: The bottling line filled 23,750 units last quarter with a defect rate of 2.4% (faulty seals and sediment), down from 3.7% a year ago. Customer complaints about cloudy oil fell from 34 to 26 per month. Average order fulfilment time is 4.3 days. Market research of 750 specialty-food shoppers found that 58% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified single-estate oil, and 47% check origin traceability before buying. 18 of 64 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filtration unit; off-the-job certification courses at the technical college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Valle Dorado Olive Oil as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.85 to $13.61 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills. (3) Olive harvest prices and bottle-glass costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and food inflation is running at 7.2%, while consumer spending on premium cooking oils grew 4.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VDO plans to fund part of its bottling-line expansion with a $650,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for VDO of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs VDO nothing in interest or dividend payments, protecting cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $288,000 a year and is committing $1,200,000 to the automated bottling and filtration line. Every dollar not paid to new shareholders stays inside the company to absorb the 9.8% rise in olive harvest and bottle-glass costs, so VDO can hold its $14.60 selling price instead of raising it for supermarket customers.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids issuing new shares, so Catalina Reyes keeps full ownership and control of VDO and no external shareholder can influence how the automated line is run or demand higher dividends. It also signals financial strength to supermarkets considering the three export contracts, and preserves the $650,000 share issue as a standby funding source if the filtration unit costs overrun or the spillage waste problem proves more expensive to fix than budgeted, and it avoids revealing commercial terms to new shareholders while VDO is still negotiating its third export market.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Valle Dorado Olive Oil and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: VDO is launching its certified single-estate range to supermarket shoppers. Consider a national television campaign, food-magazine advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VDO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A national TV slot would reach millions of viewers quickly and give the new single-estate range mass brand awareness across all three export markets. However, production and airtime costs would absorb a large share of the $1,200,000 expansion budget, and much of the audience buys value vegetable oil rather than premium extra virgin products, so wastage would be very high for a 64-employee business financing the line through a share issue and retained profit.

Food-magazine advertising: Specialist food and lifestyle magazines reach readers who actively seek premium cooking oils, and full-page features can explain single-estate origin and certification in depth, matching the 47% of 750 surveyed shoppers who check origin traceability. The drawbacks are narrow circulation, monthly frequency, and no direct way to show younger supermarket buyers the packaging story at the point of purchase, so awareness builds slowly against well-funded rival brands.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with cookery and family lifestyle influencers targets exactly the 58% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.50 more for certified single-estate oil, delivers measurable engagement, and shows the eco-friendly glass packaging story directly to younger buyers with high video quality. Results depend on influencer credibility and are slower to compound than TV, and a share of spend is lost to follower fraud, but cost per genuinely interested shopper is far lower than television.

Recommendation: VDO should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise premium segment already proven in its research, costs a fraction of television, scales across all three export markets unlike local print editions, and reinforces the origin story that 47% of shoppers check. Television is rejected as unaffordable and wasteful for a $1,200,000 expansion funded partly by retained profit; food-magazine advertising is rejected as too narrow and slow to support a 95,000-unit national launch; influencers should be layered with in-store supermarket tastings to convert reach into sales.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VDO with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VDO with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and food-magazine advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: VDO's quality complaints have reached 26 per month. Explain two benefits for VDO of using autocratic leadership to enforce consistent bottling standards in its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets VDO's Catalina Reyes set exact bottling, filtration and sealing procedures and enforce them immediately, which is valuable when defect rates of 2.4% still produce 26 complaints a month. Clear instructions remove ambiguity on the line, so every operator follows the same sediment-removal standard, protecting the supermarket export contracts that the $1,200,000 automated line depends on.

Point 2: Fast, centralised decisions suit a crisis quality problem: when complaints spike or a sealing fault is detected, VDO does not need to debate fixes through meetings, so corrective action starts the same shift and spillage waste is contained. The flat status commands also underline urgency to the 64 employees, and because the structure is hierarchical, supervisors can monitor compliance closely and report upward, giving VDO the tight control it needs while 18 staff still lack filtration training and the warehouse spillage waste keeps climbing. It also reassures supermarket auditors that VDO takes quality seriously while certification is pending, reinforcing the export-market credibility that the automated line was built to secure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VDO's complaint levels, defect rate and organisational structure.

questions.question_text: VDO must train 18 staff who have not completed filtration-unit certification. Consider on-the-job training on the line or off-the-job certification at the technical college. Which should VDO choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside experienced operators on VDO's own filtration unit is directly relevant to the exact machine settings, bottle types and eco-friendly glass packaging used in production, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 23,750-unit quarterly output and the push to cut complaints below 26 per month. The drawbacks are that experienced staff lose time from their own duties, bad habits can be passed on, and no external certificate is gained, which may not satisfy supermarket auditors who increasingly request documented competence records.

Off-the-job certification: Courses at the technical college cost $750 per employee, so 18 staff cost $13,500 in total; this is minor beside the $1,200,000 investment. Staff learn current best practice away from production pressure, gain a recognised certificate that supports ISO-style audits and export-market credibility, and return with knowledge of the science behind sediment removal rather than just machine routines. However, it removes them from the line, reducing short-term output, and the generic syllabus will not match every VDO-specific seal and filtration setting, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: VDO should choose off-the-job certification for the 18 staff, followed by short on-the-job coaching on the actual filtration unit. The $13,500 cost is trivial against $1,200,000 and against the commercial damage of 26 monthly complaints and a 2.4% defect rate on export contracts; VDO's autocratic hierarchy can schedule the two-week absence with minimal disruption, and the certificate strengthens supermarket negotiations. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it cannot produce documented externally benchmarked competence, risks inconsistent standards across three export markets, and would leave VDO unable to prove to auditors that sediment defects are systematically controlled.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training options with limited application to VDO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training options in the context of VDO.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training options in the context of VDO with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, audit and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VDO's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $288,000 ÷ ($14.60 − $8.20) = $288,000 ÷ $6.40 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.60 − $8.20 = $6.40. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VDO's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. VDO's managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 95,000 units to confirm the bottling line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 50,000 units, informing whether to retire the old line early and run the new automated plant at full capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.40 lets VDO model supermarket price negotiations: for example, a 4% price cut to $14.02 would drop contribution to $5.82, so managers can judge whether the extra volume needed to keep total contribution unchanged is realistic before signing new export contracts.
3. Fixed costs of $288,000 and contribution per unit can be used to test the affordability of the $550,000 retained profit reinvestment and the remaining $650,000 share issue proceeds, checking that the automated line generates enough contribution to service growth without overstretching cash before the March 2026 financial year closes.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($288,000 ÷ 95,000 units + $8.20 = $11.23 a unit) to benchmark performance quarter by quarter, quantify the cost of spillage waste and the 2.4% defect rate, and target purchasing negotiations on the $8.20 variable cost in response to the 9.8% olive-harvest and bottle-glass inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.40 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 50,000 units against 95,000-unit output; supermarket price-negotiation modelling from $6.40 contribution; funding checks for the $1,200,000 expansion financed by $550,000 retained profit and a $650,000 share issue; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.23 to attack the 2.4% defect rate and spillage waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VDO's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has VDO's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.69 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.98 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $150,000 trade receivables + $80,000 cash = $440,000; 2025 current assets = $180,000 + $190,000 + $95,000 = $465,000. Short-term coverage 2024 = $440,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.69; 2025 = $465,000 ÷ $235,000 = 1.98. Quick coverage excluding inventories 2024 = ($440,000 − $210,000) ÷ $260,000 = $230,000 ÷ $260,000 = 0.88; 2025 = ($465,000 − $180,000) ÷ $235,000 = $285,000 ÷ $235,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. The coverage of immediate obligations improved from 1.69 to 1.98, helped by current liabilities falling from $260,000 to $235,000 while current assets rose, and the quick coverage rose from 0.88 to 1.21, so VDO no longer depends on selling stock to meet short-term debts — vital while it beds in the $1,200,000 automated line funded by retained profit and a share issue rather than new borrowing. However, inventories fell from $210,000 to $180,000, which supports cash flow but leaves less buffer if export orders surge, and trade receivables rose from $150,000 to $190,000, tying up cash with supermarket and export customers whose payment terms could slip; if collections slow, the stronger position could deteriorate quickly even though the share issue means no new loan repayments.

Conclusion: VDO's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.69 to 1.98) and the acid test ratio (0.88 to 1.21) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not rely on inventory build-up; capital employed rose from $2,580,000 to $3,330,000 alongside non-current assets from $2,400,000 to $3,100,000, consistent with funded expansion. The residual risks are rising trade receivables and a leaner inventory balance, so VDO should tighten credit control with export customers and hold a modest stock buffer before committing the remainder of the share-issue proceeds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether VDO's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VDO of introducing eco-friendly glass packaging for its single-estate range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-friendly glass packaging reinforces VDO's positioning with exactly the 58% of 750 surveyed shoppers willing to pay up to $0.50 more for certified single-estate oil, letting VDO hold its $14.60 selling price against the 9.8% rise in olive-harvest and bottle-glass costs. Glass also signals premium quality in supermarket listings across three export markets, protects oil flavour better than plastic for extra virgin grades, and supports the $1,200,000 automated line's commercial case by winning listings that plastic-packed rivals cannot.

Disadvantage: Glass is heavier and costlier to produce and transport than plastic, raising the $8.20 variable cost per unit and cutting the $6.40 contribution unless the $0.50 premium is accepted by all supermarket buyers, not just export customers. Extra weight also increases breakage and freight damage in transit, aggravating the existing 2.4% defect rate and spillage waste problem, and any switchover downtime on the automated line would interrupt supply to supermarkets already recording 26 complaints a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VDO's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect VDO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): VDO is financed by a $650,000 share issue and $550,000 retained profit rather than a new variable-rate loan, so the direct cash hit is limited; however, higher interest raises the cost of any overdraft used for working capital while receivables stand at $190,000, and could temper supermarket and export buyers' appetite for premium orders if consumer credit tightens. The effect is real but modest, and VDO can shield itself further by avoiding variable-rate borrowing until the expansion pays back.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.61 per hour): VDO employs 64 staff, many in low-paid bottling and warehouse roles. If average hourly pay is near $13, the annual cost of one full-time worker is roughly $27,000, so a 5.9% rise adds about $1,600 per worker, or roughly $100,000 a year across the workforce — far larger than the interest-rate effect. Democratic involvement is not available under its autocratic style, so VDO must recover this through productivity on the automated line, reduced spillage waste and tighter supervision rather than through staff consultation.

Input cost inflation (9.8% olive harvest and bottle glass): VDO's variable cost of $8.20 per unit is dominated by raw materials and packaging. A 9.8% rise on those components adds roughly $0.60 to $0.80 per unit; at 95,000 units a year that is about $57,000 to $76,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $6.40 toward $5.60 to $5.80 before any price rise, and eroding the margin that justifies the $1,200,000 investment unless VDO secures the $0.50 premium from supermarkets and renegotiates supplier contracts.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 95,000 units VDO sells and removes an estimated $57,000 to $76,000 a year directly from contribution, threatening exactly the margin that services the expansion; even selling the premium range at full price, supermarket contracts may resist passing on the full increase. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious threat, adding roughly $100,000 to payroll unless automation absorbs it, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest cash impact because VDO avoided new variable-rate debt — all three, though, require VDO to prioritise cost control, price recovery and waste reduction before the April 2027 wage change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VDO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VDO's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VDO with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
